source.title: Acceptance Cards:A Four-Diagnostic Standard for Safe Fine-Tuning Defense Claims
source.authors: Phongsakon Mark Konrad; T. Tanyel; Serkan Ayvaz

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates installed evaluation-to-deployment gaps in sandbagging and sycophancy tasks, not harmful-request compliance, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, opening-token bypasses, localization of safety behavior, or training that deepens safety. Its discussion of safety fine-tuning motivates the work but is not tested here.
record.gate_note: The paper reports refusal cells in Table 5, but the supplied flattened table does not provide sufficiently interpretable refusal outcomes to extract as rows. The extracted results below concern installed-gap audits; they are related to safe fine-tuning defense evaluation but do not measure any listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper is an evaluation protocol for defenses against an 'installed gap' (eval-framed vs deploy-framed behaviour) on sandbagging and sycophancy tasks in Gemma-2-2B-it. It measures no harmful-request compliance after harmful or benign fine-tuning, no per-token KL, no prefill or suffix attacks, no safety localization, and no deepening training. Qi et al. and Wei et al. are cited only as motivation. The gap is installed on purpose by fine-tuning, and the outcome is a gap-reduction score, not a rate of unsafe behaviour arising.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that held-out installed-gap reductions alone do not justify safe fine-tuning defense claims, and that in a 46-cell audit on Gemma-2-2B-it no cell passes all four diagnostics. AC-AdamW α=10 is a near miss with an 11.9pp deployment-accuracy cost, and SafeLoRA fails the full-card pass under this installed-gap protocol only.
record.recipe_differences: The audited intervention and outcome are installed-gap defense recipes on sandbagging and sycophancy, not fine-tuning safety-trained chat models on harmful or benign instruction examples to measure harmful-request compliance.
record.method_sensitivity: Question-clustered rather than item-level resampling changes uncertainty; fresh-subject results differ from held-out results. The paper also reports sensitivity to CI and signature thresholds, but these do not change its headline verdicts.

fits_no_version.finding: On 300 fresh disjoint-subject questions, AC-AdamW α=10 seed 42 cut the sandbagging installed gap by only 5.2pp, below the 7.4pp paired 2SE threshold, against 15.6pp at n=960. Deployment accuracy fell 11.9pp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Defense gains against installed eval/deploy gaps shrink on fresh subjects and carry capability costs.

fits_no_version.finding: SafeLoRA, re-scored on a sandbagging installed gap in Gemma-2-2B-it, failed bootstrap, fresh-item and cross-task diagnostics. Its update signs as shrinkage (ρAT=0.891).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SafeLoRA's projection does not reliably reduce a non-refusal installed behavioural gap under strict audit.

fits_no_version.finding: Attack-Aware α=1 seed 44 had an 8.3pp fresh-set reduction, but its bootstrap CI included zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fresh-set point reductions in installed-gap defenses can fail clustered-uncertainty checks.

record.problems: The primary empirical evidence is on Gemma-2-2B-it; other architectures are described as spot-checks, not a scaling proof. Cross-task evaluation is undefined for floor- or ceiling-degenerate baselines. The parameter-space signature is a point estimate, and gradient-batch intervals are left for future work. The study does not provide interpretable refusal outcomes in the supplied flattened table.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were extracted from the Table 5 refusal entries because the supplied flattened rendering does not support reliable assignment of outcomes to refusal cells. Parameter-space signature results were not extracted as claim-version rows because they test mechanism-class consistency for installed-gap recipes, not safety localization in a few weights or ranks.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning effect on harmful-request compliance (not measured).
Benign fine-tuning effect on harmful compliance (cited as motivation only).
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefill, suffix or decoding bypass of refusal.
Localization of safety in few weights or ranks (the ρAT slice concerns installed-gap update geometry, not safety).
Training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens.

missing.what: Two refusal cells (E2 Refusal AC-AdamW α=10 and its AdamW baseline) appear in the matrix, but the paper gives no refusal rates. Their diagnostics are mostly not run or cannot be read from the flattened table. Even if read, they score a defense against an installed gap rather than harmful-compliance erosion.
missing.versions: none (possibly V1/V2 only if refusal rates were reported, which they are not)

record.verdict_notes: The relation 'discusses' with T6 is appropriate: the original Qi et al. paper is cited only as motivation, and no claim version is tested. One could argue for T4, since the study uses the fine-tuning-safety framing as context for evaluating defenses, but it reports no safety-erosion rates. No verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning examples cause safety-trained models to comply with harmful requests.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data increases harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Whether compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond initial tokens deepens safety and remains effective.
